Issued at 333 PM CDT Tue Oct 13 2026

The cold front from yesterday afternoon has slowly progressed 
southeastward, and has stalled out from Salina, KS northeastward to 
about Peoria, IL. South of this boundary, temperatures have climbed 
into the high 80s/low 90s, with dewpoints residing in the low 70s. 
This has increased instability along/south of the boundary to about 
2000-2500 J/kg, with effective bulk shear residing around 35-40 kts. 
This unstable, sheared airmass will see influence from a shortwave 
and strengthening LLJ later into the evening, providing synoptic-
scale lift and invigorating the development of organized 
thunderstorms. CAM guidance throughout the day has indicated an 
initial discrete mode with storms as they fire up along the 
boundary, before congealing into an MCS by the overnight period. 
More recent guidance has been varied with the exact trajectory of 
the MCS during the overnight period, but generally has placed it 
along/south of the I-70 corridor, following the boundary/CAPE 
gradient. With initial discrete storm modes, there is an associated 
hazard for large hail/damaging winds. There is an additional concern 
for isolated tornadoes, especially if storms develop near/along the 
boundary or within the proximity of the LLJ. After these initial 
discrete storm modes, damaging wind will become the primary hazard 
with the congealing MCS. 

An additional concern with storms overnight will be excessive heavy 
rainfall. PWATs of ~1.7 inches has developed across north-central MO 
throughout the day, with guidance indicating PWATs of up to 2 inches 
by the evening. Additionally, moisture transport resides just 
parallel/at a slight angle to the surface boundary, with a moist 
vertical profile in place. Although storms will remain progressive 
through the evening with strong cloud layer winds and 
upshear/downshear vectors, efficient storms training over the same 
locations will enhance concerns for flooding through the overnight, 
especially with dry antecedent conditions making it harder for soils 
to saturate right away. The current Flood Watch was expanded 
northward to include counties within the KC Metro area, as guidance 
has also increasingly trended towards higher rainfall accumulations 
during the overnight period (~2-4 inches in the HREF LPMM by early 
Wednesday). 

The severe threat is expected to diminish through the overnight as 
the environment becomes more capped and synoptic scale forcing 
diminishes. Continued moist advection over the boundary will keep 
light rain across the forecast area during the early morning, before 
it looks to also diminish by the afternoon as the boundary sags 
further south. CAMs have been varied with their resolutions of 
activity during the day tomorrow, with recent runs either placing 
additional scattered showers/storms across the area while others 
keep the forecast area dry for most of the day into the evening. 
Currently, PoPs for the day reside around 30-50% to account for the 
additional moist advection over the boundary. The primary corridor 
for continued severe hazards during the day tomorrow resides south 
of the boundary, which looks to remain just south of our forecast 
area. With uncertainty regarding the evolution of an ongoing 
flooding concern, have chosen not to extend the Flood Watch in time 
across the forecast area, with greater opportunities for excessive 
rainfall continuing to the south and west of the forecast area.

By early Thursday, the upper-level trough over the Intermountain 
West will lift towards the Great Lakes, and continue precipitation 
chances through synoptic-scale ascent with dCVA and strong low-level 
WAA. There are indications of an excessive rainfall threat with this 
next round of precipitation, with HREF LPMMs coming in a bit hot in 
swaths of high accumulations during that timeframe (~1-3 inches). 
However, this threat looks to be relatively short-lived as the 
trough quickly lifts towards the Great Lakes by the evening. As this 
trough and its attendant surface low lift off towards the 
northeast, a cold front will sweep southeast across the forecast
area and synoptic high-pressure will build in from the west. 
The cold frontal passage will help bring down temperatures to 
more seasonable temperatures, with high temperatures in the high
50s/low 60s during the daytime. Building high pressure behind 
the surface low will enhance the pressure gradient going into 
Friday, and lead to breezy conditions not too dissimilar from 
this past Monday (gusts up to 30- 35 mph possible). Building 
high pressure will also lead to synoptic- scale subsidence, 
keeping conditions dry going into the weekend. Enhanced 
radiational cooling under clear skies will allow temperatures to
drop into the 30s overnight, putting areas of northern 
MO/northeastern KS under their first frost conditions since late
